verdict: Rollout FAILED: the experiment ran, but val_bpb = 1.033115 did not improve on the current best 1.021636 by more than the required 0.0005 (lower is better).

insights_in_context.hint: Do not increase model size under a fixed compute budget; the larger model trained on too few tokens and got worse, so try a smaller/deeper-or-thinner model or a faster setup instead.

The failed deeper experiment did not justify making the model thinner, so the next experiment should avoid changing model capacity and instead test a same-size speedup or optimizer/schedule improvement.

insight.hint: You kept halving the batch size after the gains had already collapsed from ~0.056 to ~0.0024, so the curve peaked at 2^17 and the third halving cost ~0.0115 — hold the batch at 2^17 and pick a different experiment.

judge.summary: The agent continued the only successful line of the experiment history — halving the optimizer batch size — for a third time. It edited train.py to change TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE from 2**17 to 2**16 and DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE from 64 to 32 (keeping seq length 2048 and grad accumulation at 1), committed the change, and ran it via ./run.sh. The run completed cleanly (num_steps=3633, 238.1M tokens, 11.6 GB peak VRAM) but produced val_bpb = 1.033115, which is ~0.0115 worse than the current best 1.021636, so the harness discarded the run. The agent's own analysis concluded the batch-size curve has peaked at 2^17 and that future experiments should keep the batch at 2^17 and attack schedule or throughput instead.
judge.feedback: There is no code bug — the run executed correctly, but the experiment design was the first (and only) real error, made when the change was chosen and written. The agent extrapolated a linear trend from a curve that had already collapsed: per the history, the first halving (2^19 -> 2^18) improved val_bpb by ~0.056 (1.079941 -> 1.023988) and the second (2^18 -> 2^17) by only ~0.0024 (1.023988 -> 1.021636). The attempt's rationale misread this as 'both runs improved by about 0.0024', i.e. a steady marginal gain, when in fact the returns had fallen by an order of magnitude, which should have predicted the next halving to be neutral-to-negative; it was (-0.0115). A second warning sign was ignored: shrinking DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE also shrinks the per-step GPU work on a small 50M model, so throughput drops — the harness stats confirm the 2^16 run processed fewer total tokens (238.1M) than the 2^17 best (252.4M), meaning the 'more optimizer updates' came at the cost of training on ~14M fewer tokens. The correct move at the edit step was to stop halving, leave TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**17 and DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64 in place, and spend the single experiment on a different untried lever (e.g., an LR/schedule change or a throughput improvement at the current batch size).
judge.corrected_step:
import torch.nn as nn

# Batch size is NOT to be touched in this experiment: the halving trend has peaked
# (gains shrank ~0.056 -> ~0.0024 across the last two halvings, and 2**17 is the
# sweet spot for this 50M-param model), so keep TOTAL_BATCH_SIZE = 2**17 and
# DEVICE_BATCH_SIZE = 64 exactly as in the current best, and use the one
# experiment on a different, untried lever (LR/schedule or throughput).
EMBEDDING_LR = 0.6      # learning rate for token embeddings (Adam)
UNEMBEDDING_LR = 0.004  # learning rate for lm_head (Adam)
MATRIX_LR = 0.05        # learning rate for matrix parameters (Muon), 25% bump from 0.04
